Set a higher preference to the advertised prefixes for the primary or active connection. Then, set a medium or lower preference for the passive connection.\\n* AS Path prepend using a shorter AS path on the active connection and a longer AS path on the passive connection.\\n* Advertise the most specific route using BGP on the active connection.\\n\\n**Note:**\u00a0AS Path prepending can't be used to configure Active/Passive connections in the following scenarios:\\n\\n* Connection A (virtual interface VIF-A) is in Region 1.\\n* Connection B (virtual interface VIF-B) is in Region 2.\\n* Both virtual interfaces connect to a VPC in Region 1 using a Direct Connect gateway.\\n* Both virtual interfaces advertise the same prefixes with the same BGP attributes (such as AS Path and MED) on both connections from the on-premises location.\\n\\nFor these scenarios, outbound traffic from the VPC to the on-premises location prefers Connection A due to being in the same Region as the VPC. To setup Active/Passive Direct Connect connections in this scenario, apply a [local preference BGP community tag](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html#bgp-communities-private-transit). Also, you can advertise a more specific route on an active connection\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-active-passive-connection\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How can I use BGP communities to influence the preferred routing path on Direct Connect links from AWS to my network?\",\"context\":\"### Apply community tags and prepend AS\\\\_PATH attributes\\n\\nDirect Connect supports the following local preference BGP community tags:\\n\\n* 7224:7100 Low preference\\n* 7224:7200 Medium preference\\n* 7224:7300 High preference\\n\\nDirect Connect evaluates [local preference BGP community tags](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html#local-pref-bgp-communities) from lowest to highest preference.\\n\\nTo use community tags and AS\\\\_PATH attributes, take the following actions:\\n\\n* For each prefix that you advertise over a BGP session, apply a community tag to show the associated path's priority for returning traffic.\\n* When you advertise from an on-premises router to AWS, prepend additional AS\\\\_PATH attributes to the prefixes. Direct Connect prioritizes the path with the fewest AS\\\\_PATH attributes for returning traffic.\\n\\nFor example, you have virtual interfaces A and B, and you're advertising prefixes 10.10.10.0/24 and 10.20.20.0/24 to AWS. To make virtual interface A the preferred routing path for traffic to network 10.10.10.0/24, apply higher preference tag 7224:7300 to prefix 10.10.10.0/24 on the BGP session. To make virtual interface B the preferred routing path for traffic to network 10.20.20.0/24, apply higher preference tag 7224:7300 to prefix 10.20.20.0/24 on the BGP session.\\n\\nIf you don't use BGP community tags to specify local preference for private virtual interfaces, then the outbound routing behavior defaults to an AWS Region. In this case, the behavior is based on the Direct Connect location's relative distance to the originating Region. If the relative distance costs aren't equal, then [Autonomous System (AS) prepending](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/WorkingWithVirtualInterfaces.html#vif-prerequisites) can't influence routing behavior. Direct Connect evaluates the lowest distance relative cost before you prepend AS\\\\_PATH.\\n\\nTo load balance traffic across multiple AWS Direct Connect connections, apply the same community tag across the prefixes for the connections\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-bgp-communities\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Advanced Routing scenarios with AWS Direct Connect SiteLink | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"## Rule Priority\\n\\nRule 3 takes precedence over Rule 1, and Rule 1 takes precedence over Rule 2. Please note if CE2 advertises the prefix 10.0.0.0/24 to ALD1 with prepending its ASN twice then ALD1 prefers the path through CE2 compared to the path received from ALD3 (as described in Rule 1).\\n\\nFigure 7: Rule 3 preferred over Rule 1 and Rule 2 using AS path prepend.\\n\\nIn both the preceding examples, ALD1 prefers the path to the New York data center over the directly connected path to CE2, and the path using the second Direct Connect location in Sydney.\\n\\nNote that if you prepend AS path and tag your BGP Prefixes with Local preference BGP communities, then ALD evaluates the reserved community tags before AS path length. As shown in the following diagram (figure 8), both the paths ALD1 \u2192 CE2, and ALD1 \u2192 ALD2 \u2192 CE3 are tagged with the same BGP community, ALD1 prefers ALD1 \u2192 CE2 path as it has the BGP community and shorter AS path length. If that path fails, then ALD1 \u2192 ALD2 \u2192 CE3 is preferred over the ALD1 \u2192 ALD3 \u2192 CE4 path.\\n\\nFigure 8: Rule 3 preferred over Rule 1 and Rule 2 using BGP Local preference Community and AS path prepend\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/advanced-routing-scenarios-with-aws-direct-connect-sitelink/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify AWS docs on Direct Connect AS-path prepending and VIF failover behavior"}

BGP attributes include AS Path and MED\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-private-transit-interface\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Direct Connect routing policies and BGP communities\",\"context\":\"## Private virtual interface and transit virtual interface routing policies\\n\\nIf you're using AWS Direct Connect to access your private AWS resources,\\nyou must specify the IPv4 or IPv6 prefixes to advertise over BGP. These prefixes can be\\npublic or private.\\n\\nThe following outbound routing rules apply based on the prefixes advertised:\\n\\n* AWS evaluates the longest prefix length first. AWS recommends advertising\\n more specific routes using multiple Direct Connect virtual interfaces if the\\n desired routing paths are meant for active/passive connections. See Influencing Traffic over Hybrid Networks using Longest Prefix\\n Match for more information.\\n* Local preference is the BGP attribute recommended to use when desired routing\\n paths are meant for active/passive connections and the prefix lengths advertised\\n are the same. This value is set per Region to prefer AWS Direct Connect Locations that have the same\\n associated AWS Region using the `7224:7200`\u2014Medium local\\n preference community value. Where the local Region is not\\n associated with the Direct Connect location, it is set to a lower value. This\\n applies only if no local preference community tags are assigned.\\n* AS_PATH length can be used to determine the routing path when the prefix\\n length and local preference are the same.\\n* Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) can be used to determine the routing path when\\n prefix length, local preference, and AS_PATH are the same. AWS does not\\n recommend using MED values given their lower priority in evaluation.\\n* AWS uses equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing across multiple transit or\\n private virtual interfaces when prefixes have the same AS_PATH length and BGP\\n attributes. The ASNs in the AS_PATH of the prefixes do not need to match\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Direct Connect Failover Test\",\"context\":\"# Direct Connect Failover Test\\n\\nThe AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit resiliency models are designed to ensure that you have the\\nappropriate number of virtual interface connections in multiple locations. After you\\ncomplete the wizard, use the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit failover test to bring down the BGP peering\\nsession in order to verify that traffic routes to one of your redundant virtual interfaces,\\nand meets your resiliency requirements.\\n\\nUse the test to make sure that traffic routes over redundant virtual interfaces when a\\nvirtual interface is out of service. You start the test by selecting a virtual interface,\\nBGP peering session, and how long to run the test. AWS places the selected virtual\\ninterface BGP peering session in the down state. When the interface is in this state,\\ntraffic should go over a redundant virtual interface. If your configuration does not contain\\nthe appropriate redundant connections, the BGP peering session fails, and traffic does not\\nget routed. When the test completes, or you manually stop the test, AWS restores the BGP\\nsession. After the test is complete, you can use the AWS Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit to adjust your\\nconfiguration.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nDo not use this feature during a Direct Connect maintenance period as the BGP session might\\nbe restored prematurely either during or after the maintenance\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/resiliency_failover.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify AWS docs on Direct Connect prefix parity requirements for BGP failover"}

{"id": "15127dfd-ca3f-4ac3-a0c3-cb7c2468b204", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No — that's expected, working design, not a coverage gap.

Here's why: AS-path prepending on VIF-A is a standard way to build an **active/passive** setup. Since both VIFs advertise the same prefixes (10.10.0.0/24 and 10.10.1.0/24) with the same attributes otherwise, AWS evaluates local preference first, then falls back to AS-path length. With VIF-A prepended, its AS-path is longer, so AWS prefers the shorter path via VIF-B for outbound traffic — that's just VIF-B being deliberately made primary and VIF-A the backup.

The important check for failover coverage isn't the AS-path asymmetry itself — it's whether **both VIFs still carry the same prefixes with reachable next-hops**, so that if VIF-B's BGP session drops, AWS automatically falls back to VIF-A since it's the only remaining path advertising those routes. As long as:

- Both VIFs are advertising *both* /24s (not split so each VIF only owns one prefix), and
- VIF-A's BGP session is healthy and prepending is the only differentiator (not also filtering the prefixes),

...then this is correctly configured active/passive redundancy, not a gap.

One thing worth double-checking on your end: if VIF-A and VIF-B are actually in **different Regions** but both connect to the same VPC via a Direct Connect Gateway, AS-path prepending won't reliably influence outbound-from-AWS routing in that topology — AWS's Region-affinity rule can override it. If that's your setup, the "preference" you're seeing might not hold consistently, and local preference BGP community tags would be the safer mechanism instead of prepending alone.

Want me to look at the actual VIF/DXGW configuration in your account to confirm both prefixes are advertised on both interfaces and check for that cross-Region caveat?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
